subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We can hear the laughs
and the derisive comments of hon. members opposite. Certainly they were not used to such definite expressions from their leader.

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon
We remember, for instance, that the former Prime Minister and the hon. member for Quebec East, stated we ought not to raise our tariffs for fear of offending the United States. They remind me of the mother who would try to prevent the dogs from barking for fear they might awaken her baby.
Do hon. members know how those words of the present Prime Minister were explained during the last election campaign in the province of Quebec? How did they explain the expression that if necessary we would blast our way to the markets of the world? Hon. members opposite explained those words by saying that they meant a new step towards conscription. We are not surprised when they are not able to understand that the language of diplomacy may sometimes be firm and not cease to be diplomatic. History will show that our great leader was right, and anybody reading what has taken place in Canada since 1930 will acknowledge that in oertain ways Canada has blasted its way through the markets of the world.
Let us state briefly what has taken place. In 1931 we made treaties with Australia and New Zealand, so drafted that now, although New Zealand butter dealers are shipping thousands of pounds of butter to Canada, this butter remains in bond until the sale of it will not be injurious to the butter producers of Canada. We secured at the Ottawa conference of 1932 substantial and profitable preferences for our goods in all markets of the empire. We have also concluded satisfactory arrangements with Germany, in a few days we hope to conclude a satisfactory treaty with France, and we already see the dawn of the day when the United States of America will come to us and offer to lower the tariff walls which have proven so disastrous to our Canadian agricultural producers. Why should we not be proud of our achievements, why should we not boast of our accomplishments, why should we not be optimists, when our conscience tells us that we have done everything possible to help agriculture all over Canada?
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that this stabilization fund will assure more than $10,000,000 to Canadian farmers, and consequently this measure of salvation will be an additional burden on the exchequer of the country. Therefore the hon. Minister of Finance has been obliged to increase taxation, because revenues have decreased, because the deficits of the Canadian National Railways have increased to an appalling extent and because, as the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth 53719-248
has frankly admitted, in relieving unemployment the government has spent lavishly. I am pleased that the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth has made that admission, in view of the fact that this afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) said we had done nothing practically to relieve unemployment. Now, Mr. Speaker, we have to find the money for that stabilization fund, for the relief of unemployment and to continue to pay pensions to soldiers. Naturally the Minister of Finance must find it somewhere. Therefore he has decided that this year he would impose a tax on sugar. Hon. members opposite profess to be horrified. The hon. member for Quebec East, speaking in Quebec on March 28, characterized such taxation as infamous. Our Liberal friends are fond of such moderate expressions. The hon. member for Vancouver South last fall referred to the Ottawa conference agreements as "iniquitous documents." And a few weeks ago the same hon. member, when discussing the railway legislation, called it an "iniquitous bill." But now the hon. member for Quebec East wants to get first prize for using wild expressions, so he calls this sugar tax "infamous." Let us consider for a moment the various aspects of that taxation. We find that refined sugar before the war sold at ten cents a pound, and during the war it sold at even more than thirty cents a pound. Since our party came into power, whether it is because the refiners were afraid of the energetic action that the government might take in using against them the Combines Investigation Act if they tried to crush the consumer, or on account of some other cause at any rate the fact is that the refiners kept the price of sugar at about five cents per pound. Now even if we add two cents a pound tax, sugar will still be selling at three cents less than it sold before the war all over Canada. Now, Mr. Speaker, why should we wonder that the hon. Minister of Finance believed that a tax of two cents a pound could reasonably be levied on sugar, when it is recognized that such a tax can be collected at the refineries, thereby saving an enormous amount that sometimes has to be spent for the collection of taxes? I have no hesitation in saying that the principle of such a tax is just, because it causes no discrimination against any class of taxpayers. Poor people, Mr. Speaker, are certainly willing to share the burden of taxation, because they are patriotic enough to understand that a government which is spending lavishly, as the opposition says, for the relief of unemployment and for pensions, and which is burdened with a heavy deficit on the rail-

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon

ways, must find the money from some source. They are courageous enough to do their share to help the exchequer of Canada. It has been said that this tax of two cents a pound on sugar will not represent more than ten cents a week to any family, be it rich or poor. I ask you earnestly, who are the people who receive pensions in Canada, who are the people who receive relief money, who are the people receiving old age pensions, who cannot spend ten cents a week extra on sugar to help the exchequer of Canada in such times of need and depression? Mr. Speaker, those who condemn the action of the government in imposing a tax upon sugar, who call it an "infamous" tax, who take pride in imitating Robespierre and Lenin by attempting to set class against class, certainly are misjudging the sense of patriotism of the poorer classes in Canada when they accuse them of being unwilling to help the Canadian exchequer to the extent of ten cents a week. I will go further, I will say that this tax will not constitute a burden on the farmers of this country. Refined sugar is mostly used in the manufacture of candy, cakes and pastries, which are seldom purchased by our farmers in these times of depression. The tax on refined sugar will on the contrary help the farmers of eastern Canada, since this tax does not touch maple sugar and maple syrup, which last year was sold at distressingly low prices. Here we may admire the far-sightedness of the government which on the one hand helps the maple sugar producers by giving maple products the benefit of the proposed stabilization fund and on the other hand taxes refined sugar which is certainly a competitor of maple sugar products.
It is not inopportune to say a few words with respect to the maple sugar industry, which is properly called the oldest industry in Canada, and which adds much to the prosperity of the province of Quebec, and my county of Dorchester. Last year I asked the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce to help the maple sugar producers by finding ways to increase the sale of their commodity. I am pleased here publicly to thank the minister not only foT having listened to my humble views with sympathy, but also for providing this year for a publicity campaign all over Canada to stimulate the sale of maple products. This publicity campaign will be paid for in part by the maple sugar producers of the province of Quebec, in part by the Quebec government and in part by the federal government. I am pleased to tell this house that with my hon. friend for Quebec West (Mr. Dupre), the Solicitor General, I have been [Mr. Gagnon.)
in close touch with the chief of the maple industry for ithe Department of Agriculture in the Quebec government, Mr. Cyrille Vaillancourt, who, by the way, ds a native son of Dorchester and a devoted and competent official of the Quebec government. We have studied together, since I have been a member of 'this house, to find means to help the ma.ple sugar industry which unfortunately had been forsaken and abandoned in previous years. Mr. Vaillancourt is largely responsible for the revival of the maple sugar industry in Quebec. Eight years ago, he established a cooperative society of maple sugar producers, called the Quebec Maple Sugar Producers, and endeavoured to put the industry on a paying basis. In one of the pamphlets published by the Quebec government I find the following:
Before a prospective member is accepted by the society, he has to sign a contract undertaking to make his product according to the methods recommended by the society, and further, always to gather and boil his maple sap under the most sanitary conditions possible and to ship only an absolutely pure product.
Each member is given a number, and labels bearing the member's number accompany each shipment made to the society. It is thus an easy matter to check up on the producers if any attempt is made to defraud, since, when the syrup reaches the society's warehouse, it is immediately inspected and graded by officials of the Department of Agriculture.
A school is supported by the Quebec provincial government, which is attended by young men who desire to acquire a better knowledge of the best methods of manufacturing maple syrup and sugar, and a refinery has been established at Plessisville which last year received twenty thousand barrels of maple syrup, each containing thirty gallons, from the two thousand members of this cooperative society. I am glad to say that chemists are at the disposal of the government, who devote their researches to the improvement of the product. A new refining plant has been established at Valley Junction, near my county, and I am glad to say that this government helped in the construction of that plant in 1931 under the unemployment relief scheme. This will be a great benefit to the maple sugar producers in my county and in the municipality of Valley Junction. I should like to thank the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) who supported my humble efforts to have the government cooperate with the province of Quebec and the municipality in the construction of this plant.
May I add that since we have been in power we have lost no opportunity to help the maple sugar industry. In December of 1930, for instance, we put into force by proclamation the Maple Sugar Industry Act and

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
Regulations which, in a letter to myself dated March 4, 1932, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) described as follows:
The Maple Sugar Industry Act and Regulations . . . became effective one year ago. It benefits the industry by prohibiting the adulteration of maple products, by establishing standards of quality, by requiring sanitary conditions in sugar camps and processing plants, and by requiring proper identification of table syrups or sugars which resemble or imitate the pure maple products. The fruit branch, charged with the administration of this act, has conducted some educational work in regard to maple products which, with the administrative work in regard to the act, will undoubtedly stimulate the interest of the producers in the production of quality products and tend to increase the demand for maple syrup and sugar, not only from the housewife but from manufacturers of ice cream, confections, etc.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, the inclusion of maple sugar products under the proposed stabilization fund will prove a substantial help to the industry, but on this side of the house we propose to do more to encourage the maple sugar producers in Canada. Last fall, for instance, just after the Imperial conference, Mr. Vaillancourt went to England, where he succeeded in organizing successful exhibitions of maple products in London, Liverpool, Plymouth and Glasgow, Scotland'. He even went to France, where he tried to promote the sale' of 'Canadian maple products. I have several times requested this government to cooperate with the provincial government of Quebec in that regard by enacting new tariff regulations which will prove more favourable to the sale of maple products in England and France. I understand that within a few days we hope to conclude a new trade treaty with France, and I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) to take the necessary steps to see that Canadian maple sugar and syrup are allowed free entry to the French market. At the same time I would ask the minister to open negotiations with the British government in order that our maple products may secure a more favourable rate of duty. It is true that Canadian maple sugar and syrup enjoys a preference on the British market at present, but I would ask that the necessary steps be taken to ensure the entry of Canadian maple products to the British market free of duty.
I do not like to detain the house too long, but I had three reasons for bringing up these points. The first was to prove to my constituents in the county of Dorchester, many of whom are engaged in the maple sugar industry, that this government is doing its best to 53719-248J
help them. My second purpose was to show that the government was extremely willing to cooperate with the provincial authorities, and in the third place I wanted to prove to the house that the imposition of a tax on refined sugar would be very helpful to the producers of maple products in Canada. These producers are not only in the province of Quebec; there are a great many of them in the province of Ontario and in the maritime provinces as well.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with what was said by the brilliant member who just sat down (Mr. Gagnon) with regard to the banking commission, the lowering of the legal rate of interest and the bonusing of wheat, but I hope he will pardon me if I do not follow him in the rest of his remarks, because of the time limit that has been imposed upon me by a rule of this house.
I do not think a single member of this chamber will disagree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), when he says that the world is approaching full realization of the fact that the day of national self-sufficiency is past, that an international disease can be cured only by an international remedy. The remedy for Canada's ills, however, must be sought both internally and externally; indeed I think all the countries in the world must take steps not only to put their own houses in order but to advance the cause of mutual cooperation among all nations before the world can enjoy if not greater prosperity then at least some semblance of the prosperity that existed prior to 1929; but in order to attain this goal the obstacles standing in the way first must be removed.
It has been said that many of our troubles are the result of the great war and that the various countries cannot rehabilitate themselves unless there is a cessation of martial strife and dissension. The desire for peace is general, Mr. Speaker, but, like the weather, everyone is talking about it and no one is doing anything about it. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) soon will depart to Washington to confer with President Roosevelt and the Prime Minister of Great Britain, and so I believe the right hon. gentleman should do everything in his power to bring about those conditions that are essential to peace. At the present time the world is clamouring for peace but there is no peace. It is also awaiting the return of prosperity but there is no prosperity. We cannot have prosperity with-

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
out the propagation and the realization of peace, neither can we maintain peace without an application of the contributing factors or conditions essential thereto, nor a return of prosperity without the cultivation of the peaceful arts and pursuits incidental thereto that are so obligatory during a period of reconstruction in the midst of which all countries find themselves to-day.
It is said, Mr. Speaker, that a prolonged period of sickness usually is followed by an even more prolonged period of convalescence. We have had a sickness lasting four years, and if that dictum is true it will be another ten years before we are completely out of this depression. In the past four years financial stringency and economic chaos have brought out the reality of the interdependency of nations in much bolder relief than ever and have emphasized the utter impossiblity in this great age of industrial development of any country living unto itself. Even in the United States, where such pet phrases as "self-contained nation," "splendid isolation" and "no foreign entanglements," were so long in vogue, the president has put himself on record in regard to the interrelationship of the constituent parts of the world and the dependence of America's future on the successful solution of universal economic troubles.
As regards Canada and the United States, I am of the opinion that our troubles can be traced directly back to Europe, where the present conditions in this country have for the most part originated. I believe that for immediate causes we must refer to the lack of purchasing power of our customers overseas. There is no doubt that if Europe cannot buy, America cannot sell, Canada's difficulties have been greatly enhanced by the fact that she is largely an exporting country, especially of wheat and other agricultural products. For many decades the European market has absorbed the exportable surplus thereof, but of late years accumulating bankruptcy consequent upon the last great war has left this great .market of ours, Europe, so weak and impoverished as to make it quite impossible to maintain anything like that trade which the European market used to call forth in pre-war days. For things have come to a pass, as has been suggested by the Minister of Finance and by the president of the United States, whereby our neighbour's troubles are merged with our own difficulties, and where the latter cannot be solved without simultaneous solution of the former.
The duty of governments, to my way of thinking, must necessarily be twofold-stabilfMr. Luchkovich.]
ization and improvement of both internal and external relations. Now, domestic conditions must be met with some new form of adaptability, whether monetary or otherwise. National stability is essential, but so is international stability; but in order to maintain the former the nations are adopting at the present time methods which simultaneously destroy the vital mechanism of international exchange. The Minister of Finance has announced with great pride a favourable balance of some $70,000,000 odd; in other words, while imports were being restricted exports nevertheless were expanding, creating the aforementioned balance. If nations are as interdependent as the Minister of Finance pointed out in the introductory remarks of his budget address, I do not see how he can logically advocate interdependence and favourable trade balances at one and the same time; for I do not see how all countries, together and at the same time, can send out greater exports and take in fewer imports. Every debit still requires a credit, and it is a physical impossibility for all countries simultaneously to have a favourable balance of trade or even of payments.
I have referred to Europe as our great customer and have casually mentioned the obstacles that bar the way to trade with said continent. A manifesto issued by two hundred bankers and manufacturers representing all the nations of the world has this to say:
It is difficult to view without dismay the extent to which tariff barriers, special licences and prohibitions since the war have been allowed to interfere with international trade and to prevent it from flowing in its natural channels.
The break-up of great political units in Europe dealt a heavy blow to international trade. Across large areas, in which the inhabitants had been allowed to exchange their products freely, a number of new frontiers were erected and jealously guarded by customs barriers. Old markets disappeared. Racial animosities were permitted to divide communities whose interests were inseparably connected.
To mark and defend these new frontiers in Europe, licences, tariffs and prohibitions were imposed with results which experience shows already to have been unfortunate for all concerned. One state lost its supplies of cheap food, another its supplies of cheap manufacture. Industries suffered for want of coal, factories for want of raw materials. Behind the customs barriers new local industries were started, with no real economic foundation which could be kept alive in the face of competition by raising the barriers higher still. . . . Too many states, in pursuit of false ideals of national interests, have imperilled their own welfare and lost sight of the common interests_ of the whole world by basing their commercial relations on the economic folly which treats all trading as a form of war.

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
There can be no recovery in Europe till politicians in all territories, old and new, realize that trade is no war, but a process of exchange, that in time of peace our neighbours are our customers and that their prosperity is a condition of our own wellbeing. If we check their prosperity, their power to purchase our goods is reduced.
It is expected that the Prime Minister of this country will attend the world economic conference some time this spring or next summer, and that 'he will exert the weight of his influence to help to restore some stability to the situation overseas. As a great exporting nation we need that market very badly; for every restriction and curtailment of our foreign trade must react most disastrously on O'ur primary producers, whose whole existence depends practically on the profitable sale of t'heir products in markets abroad. At the present time there is no profit in farming in Canada. All operations are on the debit side of the ledger. It is thus impassible to continue an such a basis, for unless the trade situation improves and better methods of distributing our products are evolved, agriculture in this country is bound to be ruined; and when an industry like agriculture fails, at is bound to have serious and adverse repercussions and reactions on all other industries in Canada.
It is folly to deny the worldwide nature of the depression and that the crisis in Canada is due to the breakdown of our own foreign markets. It is equally futile to ignore the existence of vast domestic problems that call for immediate solution in Canada and the necessity of setting our own house in order so that we might adjust ourselves more effectively to world conditions. In stressing the influence of world conditions, I hope that we in this country are not seeking an alibi for Canada's lack of policy; for this reference emanates from a realization [DOT]that trade is not war but a process of exchange. Trade being essentially barter, debts can be paid in the long run only in goods, and we cannot continue to sell abroad without buying from abroad. In spite of the fact that science has accomplished wonders in making the world a harmonious whole, extreme nationalism the world over has managed to divide it, as it were, into many parts and to keep it from forming any close alliance which would react beneficially not only to each component part but to the collective whole as well.
There is no doubt that the problem arising out of the wheat situation has been made harder to solve by the futile attempt at selfsufficiency being made by such nations as Germany and Italy. These countries have
attempted an artificial stimulation of industries for which they are not fitted. Wheat growing is not a natural industry for a country like Germany. Her soil is not adapted to it, yet every effort is being made to encourage production through the bonusing of German farmers and the raising of high tariff barriers against other countries. In this act of intense economic nationalism Germany has been actuated by a desire to make herself independent of other nations in case of war which seems to be looming everywhere upon the horizon in Europe. I think the experiment has proven to be too costly. It is far more economical to import wheat from countries where it can be produced more cheaply and exchanged for the cheaper manufactures of other countries. It may be an exaggeration of the case, but what would we think of Canada trying to produce under hothouse conditions an independent crop of bananas or oranges when these products can be brought in from other countries where their cultivation is indigenous to the locality and where the cost of production and the ultimate sale price make it more desirable as an export than as a domestic product? Wheat raising has always been indigenous to this country. With her favourable climate, with her progressive people and with her fertile soil, there is no place in the world where a better grain product can be produced than in Canada. Wheat is now our great staple export product. In 1929, the peak year of prosperity, nearly forty per cent of our total exports valued at more than half a billion dollars were grain products. It was through the grain trade that Canada reached her peak of prosperity and it is through the same trade that Canada will regain her prosperity. This is the problem which Canada's representatives at the forthcoming world economic conference must undertake to solve successfully. The present economic condition of Canada, especially in the west, is so precarious that further delay will be serious.
I agree with the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) when he includes the tariff as one of the disturbing factors in trade recovery and I agree especially with his reference to the multilateral agreements which are essential to tariff revision. One country cannot do it alone by means of a unilateral agreement but all countries acting in unison and cooperation can do a great deal in this regard. Therefore, let us hope that the economic conference will be the means of bringing about these changes without any further delav

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
Canada with her meagre force under arms and her four thousand miles of undefended boundary should be an example to the rest of the world, especially to Europe, now torn by stress and bitter racial animosity, of the benefits of disarmament, of the virtues of peace as the essential conditions of prosperity. When one realizes that during the last war 65,000000 men were mobilized and out of 37,000,000 casualties, 9,000,000 died, that the cost of the war is now rapidly approaching $100,000,000,000, these figures will give some idea of the devastating effects of warfare upon the morale and economic conditions of a country. The manhood which has been, destroyed cannot readily be replaced and its disappearance has left a void which has had a terrible reaction upon the spiritual and economic wellbeing of the world. There cannot be prosperity without peace, and peace is unlikely without disarmament. Therefore, I feel that the forthcoming visit of our Prime Minister to other lands should have something to do with this all-important subject. I am reminded of an allegorical story which I read recently in a magazine. Some worms and caterpillars in a chicken yard decided to have a conference with the chickens, and for this purpose they appointed a committee. This committee was well equipped with logic and with oratory but it did not know how to speak the chicken language, so they were forthwith gobbled up. Chicken yards are bad places for worms. There is no question that a heavily armed nation will use its instruments of war to defeat an unprotected nation, and to reduce it to subservient slavery and national oblivion. The only alternative is peace through disarmament.
The stagnating influence of war debts is too obvious to require any extended explanation at the present time. There are many reasons for drastic reductions, the most important of which is the fact that war debts are a great impediment to the recovery of prosperity. So many anomalous situations have arisen since the war that it has become impossible to pay, no matter what the good faith of the [DOT]nations may be. There are three ways in which payment can be made: first, by goods and services; second, by the proceeds of a loan, and, third, by the movement of gold. Owing to the terrific fall in the wholesale price level, it has become necessary to pay in increasingly larger quantities of goods and services; the precariousness of the economic situation has made it harder both to secure md to pay a loan, and the disequilibrium of

gold and its concentration in few hands has made it impossible to pay balances in that standard. War debts are a dead asset; they are not a productive asset as railways and the sooner they are wiped out the better it will be for the world generally. I should like to quote a little passage by Walter Lippman as follows:
There will be no economic stability until there is peace, and the world war is not over while the question of reparations and war debts is still alive. If the world can make peace and settle war debts and reparations, there will be such a return of confidence that prices will rise permanently.
The real point is tiha,t the countries still on the gold standard, the United States and France, have forced other countries to deflate and this deflation has forced down prices. If such emergencies were managed more scientifically by a controlled currency .there would be mo need for the sad state of affaire which we have in the world to-day. lit is essentially a monetary and credit crisis, the fundamental cause of which can be given in the words of a New England weekly-a systematic creation and increasing disparity between physical means of production and financial means of consumption. We know how to produce and can produce in apparently limitless quantifies, but where we fall down is in distribution. Our system is operated for profit, and when that element or motive fails, the whole structure topples over like a house of cards. Can one imagine thousands of cattle being burned, shiploads of coffee and oranges being dumped into .the sea and other products deliberately destroyed because of the lack of profitable markets and efficient methods of distributing our superabundance of goods to a starving consuming public? But tha/t is exactly what is happening in profit-making capitalistic civilization to-day where human values are sacrificed for individual gain and the ideal of service is superseded by the pursuit of economic reward.
If the government persists in laying the blame for this depression on the international situation and in seeking an international remedy to cure an international disease, then they should at least make some move in this direction. The Prime Minister of course might ask for -a complete revision of the Versailles treaty, the remaking of the map of Europe, not in accordance with the vindictive spirit of the makers of this treaty, but on the basis of justice and ethnic principles, such as race, religion and language of the inhabitants involved. The gnawing bitterness, the smouldering fires and antagonisms that

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
prevail so persistently throughout that greatest of our markets are mostly due to the forcible suppression of 'the various nationalities. This, I think, is 'the key to the situation. We should do everything possible to create ethnographical boundaries and to allow the self-determination of the nations in that greatest market of ours in keeping with their innate traditions and aspirations. The Prime Minister will realize bow extremely galling it is for these people to live in continual physical and spiritual subjugation and forced negation of the very qualities which are considered a virtue in those who rule but a sin in those who unfortunately come under domination. My observation has been that these people somehow will not stay down, and as history has given us countless examples of the folly of forcible suppression, I [DOT]think nothing but a guaranty of autonomy and liberty of cultural development will free Europe from its potential menaces to peace and well-being.
At 'the present time all those races ore more interested in political than economic liberation. They all wish to be treated as equals and not as inferiors, but once the former object is attained, they will then be unhampered in their cooperation in the latter. As matters stand, economic liberation is subordinated to political liberation, for the races seem determined to free themselves politically even if their efforts meet with untold misery, suffering and spiritual degradation. All these realities must be taken into consideration before the status of Europe is finally decided. The united states of Europe is a most desirable object for the economic salvation of that continent, but it con be attained only when all those races enter such a union voluntarily and are accepted as equals.	_
The era through which humanity has just passed might be called the age of frenzied finance. The next stage therefore will logically be one of stabilization and social control. I think the laissez-faire, rampant individualism of the past must give way to greater socialization under government supervision. The decay of vigorous predatory imperialism brought about by the awakening of the economic energies of undeveloped countries and the reduction of international trade to the interchange of products required by the mere difference in resources, climate or racial habits, the disintegration of our political situation and a host of minor problems have forced a reorientation of thought and a revaluation of ideas arising out of the realities of present day conditions.
Once again, the science of economics, being dynamic, has become subject to change. As in many other matters, so in this case nothing is ever learned definitely and completely and so the methods of the past century cannot be applied to twentieth century conditions. The present budget does not offer any solution for our difficulties beyond retrenchment, drastic economies, increased taxation, sanctity of contractual obligations and a policy of let well enough alone. But even in the case of drastic economy and taxation, the burden and incidence thereof might have been placed equally on those higher up rather than on those least able to pay. In times like these and under the present system new taxation cannot be avoided, but there should be more equality in the sacrifice. No one will quarrel with the desire for equal sacrifice, but as drastic economies and retrenchment will not solve the problem of unemployment and farm relief, one must look to more fundamental remedies for a solution.
The minister mentioned relaxation of exchange and other excessive restrictions on international trade, stabilization of currencies and stimulation of a rise in wholesale prices as fit topics for discussion at the next economic conference. He might also have added the inadequacy of gold as a metal standard as regards both quantity and efficacy, and the general problem of financial credit as the pivot of the whole economic structure. Economists are in agreement that the problem of the price level is the most important single one of our age and that low prices are due to deflation of credit. Mr. Cassel has pointed out that progressive deflation is grinding our national economy to pieces and that unless something is done to stop the process, it will mean the ultimate ruination of our country. There must be some antidote to the destructive policy of deflation, and if inflation will supply this function, as I think controlled inflation should, then I see no valid reason why it should not be employed.
Mere policies of retrenchment and aimless, hopeless groping in the dark will get us nowhere; unless governments try to do something to pierce through the economic fog in which we are at present enveloped and bring to light some constructive policy, ultimate collapse cannot be avoided. It may be good tactics to raise the bogy of contractual obligations and the sanctity of the bond, but why the bondholders should be placed in a different category from that in which others are situated is, in my opinion, very hard to justify. The Minister of Finance has spoken of equality

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
of sacrifice; why should other classes be more amenable than are the bondholders? In a period of progressive deflation I do not see why the prosperity of the average man should be subordinated to the greed and avarice of a few moneylenders. As far as the average man is concerned, deflation has knocked the bottom out of every vestige of prosperity he ever enjoyed, and it has destroyed the equity in whatever property he may at any time have owned. It has put about 1,500,000 Canadians on relief. As a recent writer put it, to-day the average man thinks not of prosperity but of a job, not of profits but of wages. But a search for one or the other is like hunting for the needle in the proverbial haystack. Hon. members may perorate as much as they like about the virtues of individualism. But, Mr. Speaker, what is there left of opportunity to the average man? I think that even such men as Lord Strathcona and Mr. Bboth, those individual giants of the past, would not get very far with their individualism and their initiative at the present time.
An lion, member has asked what the duty of a government is. Adam Smith said the duty of any government is to increase the wealth of its people. In the absence of opportunities for employment the state is faced with the necessity of assuming the responsibility for the subsistence of its citizens. With the right to such subsistence must also go the imposition of the duty to work. This, of course, will require social and economic planning on a very much larger scale. How it can be done without the inflation of our currency and without simultaneously launching a constructive public works program is very hard to understand. Up to the present time the government has managed to avert responsibility of control of industry-I speak not of one government but of governments throughout the world. However, the inevitable trend of the times lies most certainly in the direction of government control. Mr. G. D. H. Cole had this to say:
Parliaments, if they are to survive as sovereign, have to find ways of bringing the economic life of the nations under their effective control; for this economic life is crying out for organization, for national and economic planning. And if parliaments resign this task into other hands they will, under modern conditions, be throwing away the substance of authority, and keeping only the shadow.
Much has been said in this house and out of it about the glories of individual initiative and private industry. If private industry is as has been pictured, why is it that all the 
wrecks and derelicts thereof must be taken care of not only by this government but by all governments? Why is it that even ablebodied men and women cannot secure work in private industries? Hon members in both major parties do not want inflation, but certainly with the continuation of deflation, higher taxation, higher interest rates and other charges, diminishing purchasing power and increasing unemployment, I do not see how it can be avoided.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. On section 2-Declaratory.

What is
the purpose of having this work declared to be for the general advantage of Canada?

speechtext: Because it is international work.

Section agreed to.
Sections 3, 4 and 5 agreed to.
On section 6, subsection 1-Capital stock.

I should
like to ask the promoter of the bill if he thinks $25,000 is a sufficiently large paid up capital upon which to commence operations. It seems to me to be ridiculously low.

Samia-Port Huron Tunnel

The hon. member will note
that that sum is merely a deposit left as security with the government. The hon. member is reading subsection 2, which refers to the deposit guaranteeing that the work will be proceeded with. It has nothing to do with the capital stock mentioned in subsection 1.
Is there any provision in the bill stating how much shall be paid up before the work is commenced?

The hon. member for Argenteuil will note that under section 21 of the bill the Dominion Companies Act shall apply, so far as it is not inconsistent with the special provisions of this bill. Therefore my opinion is that with respect to the commencement of business and the amount required to be paid up before the commencement of business the Dominion Companies Act shall apply.

There is
nothing in the Companies Act which requires any amount to be paid up, with the exception of the corporation shares.

There used to be a provision for ten per cent. As I understand it, that provision was eliminated in 1930. At the present time there is a provision that a certain amount-I realize it is not very large -must be paid. I do not see why we should go beyond the provisions of that act when we are considering the amount to be paid up under this bill.
Have all the subsections with the exception of numbers 1 and 2 been struck out of the original bill?

The whole bill has been
reprinted. If the hon. member has a reprinted bill he will find the proposed changes underlined, and in italics on the page opposite he will see the sections as they appeared in the original bill.
Section 6, subsection 1, agreed to.
On section 6, subsection 2-Deposit before commencing operations, etc.

If this company is granted a charter, I know nothing in the Companies Act -which will force them to put up any substantial sum before beginning operations. When, a company has power to issue bonds to the value of $5,000,000, it certainly should put up a substantial sum before actually beginning work. A large enterprise such as this should have substantial backing.
I do not know- who the incorporators are, or whether they are men of large means able to carry on an undertaking of this magnitude, but I suggest there should be a provision for a large amount to be paid up before the company begins business.

Is the right hon. gentleman
discussing subsection 1 of section 6, or subsection 2.
Subsection 2.

Subsection 2 provides only for a deposit being put up in good faith by the company. It merely provides that the company shall not commence its operations or incur any liability before a sum of at least $25,000 has been paid into the treasury of the Dominion of Canada, which sum shall not be withdraw-n until at least twenty-five per cent of the proposed subway or tunnel together with its approaches, buildings, and all other assets used in connection therewith is constructed, and such sum shall be forfeited if the project is not proceeded with. In my opinion subsection 2 is merely a guarantee that when commenced, the work will be proceeded with, and if not the moneys will be forfeited to the crown. I submit subsection 2 has nothing whatever to do with subsection 1, which deals with the capital stock of the company. With respect to the amount to be paid up under subsection 1, I again submit that we are under the Dominion Companies Act, w-hich has withstood the experience of time.

I am sorry I have not the Companies Act before me, but if the hon. member has I wish he would read the provision contained therein in regard to paying up capital stock before the commencement of work.

As a matter of fact I have
only the revised statutes of Canada, 1927. Subsection 8 of section 9 of the Companies Act states:
In no case shall the amount of capital with w-hich a company shall carry on business be less than the sum of $500.

That is
the only limitation suggested?

Yes, as it exists now. The
ten per cent provision is now out, and as I understand it under the Dominion Companies Act there is only now the $500 limitation.
Sarnia-Port Huron Tunnel

The hon. gentleman says this is the course usually followed in private bills relating to private companies, but I submit for his consideration that although this is a private bill it is far from being a private company. This is going to be a public corporation, an international enterprise, for the building of an expensive tunnel. I know that some very unfortunate things have happened in connection with a bridge further down the river, built not long ago, in connection with which bonds were sold which now have comparatively little value because I suppose there was not sufficient money put up for stock ahead of the bonds to give them some value outside of the actual tunnel itself.

I agree with what the hon. gentleman says. To meet that very difficulty, at the suggestion of the Justice department we have incorporated in this bill subsection A of section 7, and I submit that it will meet with the approval of the hon. gentleman and meet the objection he has now raised. It is a new clause:
7a. No securities whether shares of stock, bonds, debentures or other securities shall be issued by the company unless and until the governor in council has been satisfied that the company has, in respect of such securities, complied with "The Securities Act" of the province of Ontario.
That is what is popularly known in Ontario as the Security Frauds Prevention Act. I hope and trust that will meet the hon. gentleman's objection.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Bonding powers.

There is a slight change in this section, therefore I will read the whole section:
7. The company may issue bonds, debentures or other securities to an amount not exceeding five million dollars in aid of the construction of the said subway or tunnel authorized by this act; and such bonds, debentures or other securities shall be secured by deed of mortgage; and such deed of mortgage shall contain provisions that all tolls and revenues derived from the use of said .subway or tunnel by other corporations or persons shall be specially charged and pledged as security for the payment of interest on such security.

Section agreed to.
On section 7, subsection A-Issue of securities.

Would the promoter be good enough to tell the committee just what are the safeguards for the public under the Securities Act of Ontario?
[Mr. Gray.l
I wish to take issue with my hon. friend as to my being the promoter.
I apologize -the sponsor.

Thank you. As I understand the act it has to do with the registration of any broker or issuer of stock before stocks or bonds or debentures can be issued. The provisions of the act require registration and licensing to sell, and in its very nature the suggestion of licensing must mean protection as far as possible to the public. In order that we may ensure compliance with that provision, this subsection is inserted.

Subsection agreed to.
Sections 8, 9 and 10 agreed to.
Ou section 11-Powers.

11. The company may,

(a) lay out, construct, complete, maintain, work, manage and use the said subway or tunnel under the St. Clair river, for vehicular, pedestrian, railway and other purposes, with the necessary approaches from convenient points on the Canadian side of the international boundary between the United States of America and the Dominion of Canada in or near the city of Sarnia, the township of Sarnia and the township of Moore, to points in or near the city of Port Huron, and the city of Marysville, in the state of Michigan, one of the United States of America.

On section 14-Expropriation.

Very large powers are being given to a private company under this bill. It occurs to me that they are rather unsusual powers to be given to a company of this kind. While the provisions of the Railway Act are made to apply, I should think that that is not all the safeguard that should be made applicable in such a bill as Ibis. Giving to a private company which is promoted for private gain the power to take the property of others against their will is something which should be done very sparingly by any legislature. I can remember a long series of battles over this very same sort of thing. While it is necessary in railway development or in works of great public utility to give this power, there is strong objection to giving it to such a company as this, which is

Sarnia-Port Huron Tunnel
not in the same category as a railway or other public utility. I for one object to the powers of expropriation that are given under this bill.

Section agreed to.

On section 19-Municipalities may purchase tunnel.

No doubt the intention of this section is that the municpalities may have the opportunity, at some time in the future, to purchase this tunnel, but I would suggest that in the third line the word "value" be replaced with the word "cost." The value might be ascertained with the company considered a going concern, having no regard to the cost of the undertaking.
I have no objection to that change.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is a very serious section. Air. Chairman, and in the form in which it now stands I think the committee should hesitate to pass it. Whatever else should be done at least we should exercise what jurisdiction we have within our powers, ostensibly at any rate. I do not think we have any power to say the board of arbitration shall have power to fix the cost or the value if one of the members of the board is without the jurisdiction of this country.
Is that the suggestion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. The section declares :
The board shall consist of three members, one to be appointed by the city of Sarnia or the municipality within the Dominion of Canada in which the portion of the said subway or tunnel in Canada may be constructed, one by the city of Port Huron or the municipality within the Lhiited States of America in which the portion of the said subway or tunnel in the United States of America may be constructed and the third by the company.
In this section the tunnel is dealt with as an entity, both ends being united as one, whereas in the previous sections the statute makes it clear beyond doubt that we do not endeavour to exercise jurisdiction beyond the centre of the stream. I am bound to say that I do not think the section as it now stands is one we have power to pass.

I understand the point raised by the right hon. gentleman. I am not particularly' enamoured of the section in any shape or form. As the hon. member for East Essex suggests, apparently the intention of the section was to have some recapture clause in the bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And there should be one.

As the right hon. gentleman points out, there should be one. I would be quite content to have the section wiped out if it were not for the suggestion of the Prime Minister that some recapture clause should be placed in the bill. If the right hon. gentleman retains that point of view I suppose there is no alternative but to have the section stand, otherwise I am quite prepared to agree to the deletion of the section.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
During the last two
months my attention 'has ibeen directed to the somewhat similar provisions of the statute concerning the bridge lower down, and if my attention had not been directed to that perhaps I would not have read 'this bill so closely. It does seem to me that it is perhaps desirable that there should be some form of what has been familiarly called-though it is not technically correct-a recapture clause in a bill such as this. I think the hon. member for East Essex has put his finger upon the real difficulty, the question of fixing t'he actual cost of the undertaking early in its period of operation. We are familiar with proceedings that have taken place in connection with matters of this kind in which the value bears no relation whatever to the cost, the value being determined largely by the earnings and the percentage of the return upon the investment. When. I heard the hon. gentleman from East Essex make his observations with regard to value I thought that was very important, but I -think the bon. member will agree that the section must be recast. As it stands now it undertakes to do something which I fear we have not 'the power to do, and I suggest that it might be better to have a section stating that the cost of the undertaking must 'be made clear to the satisfaction of the governor in council, and that should be lodged with the Department of State, and then the provisions as to recapture might be dealt with.

Then I would suggest that
the section stand.
Section stands.
On section 20-RB., c. 170, to apply to the company.

speechtext:

On section 22-Labour and materials.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think my bon. friend
may find a little difficulty here. The section.
reads:
So far as it may be practicable to do so. Canadian labour and materials must be used in the construction of the said subway or tunnel. . . .
He may find a little difficulty in connection with that provision in the state of Michigan.

This section has been included in all international bridge and tunnel bills since 1929 or 1930. It may be, as the Prime Minister says, that it is more a pious hope and prayer than something that will be of practical benefit. The intention is that, in so far as we do not overlap the international boundary, so far as the approaches to the subway or tunnel are concerned, we shall use Canadian labour and material in the work that is done. If our American friends do not like the section, then I suppose they will object to it; but in the meantime I am rather surprised that the right hon. gentleman should object that as far as possible we are protecting Canadian labour and material.
fMr. Bennett. 1

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
How unfair the hon.
gentleman is. The remark is rather cheap. I directed his attention to the fact that the bill as it now stands undertakes to legislate The Fair Wages and Eight Hour Day Act, 1930, to apply to the United States, which it cannot do. The section reads:
The employment of labour in the construction, maintenance and supervision of the said subway or tunnel shall be subject to the terms and conditions of The Fair Wages and Eight Hour Day Act, 1930.
Just as the congress of the United States would not undertake to legislate with respect to the Dominion of Canada, so we should not undertake to legislate with respect to the United States; and because I direct attention to that fact the hon. gentleman, with a cheap sneer, says he is surprised that I should object to Canadian labour and material being used. That is unworthy of him; let me say that to him at once.
I apologize if-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have given every possible assistance in connection with this legislation, and I was merely pointing out that it is not desirable that this dominion should leave the impression abroad that it is endeavouring to legislate in a country over which it has no legislative jurisdiction.
I had no intention of arousing-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
not arousing anything.

-any suspicion of a sneer. I was not sneering. As the right hon. gentleman says, he has given every assistance and afforded every opportunity to have the bill presented and passed. This section was discussed at great length in the committee, and the committee thought that as far as practicable it should be insisted upon that Canadian labour and material be used in the construction of every international bridge or tunnel. There is an international half of the construction over which we have control and an international half which is under the control of congress. We are providing against the fact that there may be overlapping by declaring that as far as practicable we shall use Canadian labour and material in our section, and apply to the work carried on in that section The Fair Wages and Eight Hour Day Act, 1930. Surely that has only to do with the Canadian section of the tunnel. I hope the Prime Minister will not find fault with the section. The committee gave it considerable

Samia-Port Huron Tunnel
thought and at the suggestion of the hon. member for London (Mr. White) and one of the members for Vancouver it was insisted that it should be made compulsory that Canadian labour and material be used.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will look at the section he will see that the practicability is the test with respect to the use of Canadian labour and material, and properly so. But in a statute of the dominion we are providing that:
The employment of labour in the construction, maintenance and supervision of the said subway or tunnel shall be subject to the terms and conditions of The Fair Wages and Eight Hour Day Act, 1930.
They shall be subject-shall be-to the terms of a Canadian statute, and I only desire, being responsible for the bill in the narrow sense of the government's responsibility for the legislation of this house, that it should not be said that we had passed a statute in which we undertook to provide that a Canadian act, an act of this parliament, should govern the construction of this work. If the hon. gentleman would add words indicating that the provision had reference to the Canadian section of the tunnel, I could understand it. That was what I was painting out.
I should not think that in this act we were legislating with reference to anything but the Canadian section.
It says differently, in terms. The forepart of the section distinctly comprehends the whole operation.
But we could not legislate, and the minister knows we could not possibly legislate, with respect to anything except the Canadian section.
Why try to do so, then?
We are not doing so, I submit. However, if it is desired for clarity's sake to insert, "in so far as the Canadian section is concerned," or words to that effect, I see no objection to doing so.

We are all trying to assist the hon. member, and if the bill is desirable, as I assume it is, it seems to me that he would meet with an insuperable barrier when he approached the government of the United States, where there must be a companion bill, if they found in our legislation th'at the whole subway and tunnel must be built subject to our Canadian laws in relation to the matter set out in the section. It is with the desire to assist the hon. member that the observations have been made. As the section reads,
it implies that our law is to apply to the whole building of the tunnel. Obviously therefore, unless the hon. member has some idea of what congress may do, this section will be an insuperable barrier to his operations later on, unless it is altered.
I suggest, then, Mr. Chairman, that after the word tunnel there be added the words "in so far as the Canadian section is concerned."

Has the
hon. member received any opinion from the Department of Justice or from any other source as to the constitutionality of the whole section?
I can only say that I have looked at similar bills passed in which there was a provision such as this-bills passed on two or three occasions.

I don't
dispute that.

maintopic: BOARD OF TRADE OF THE CITY OF TORONTO-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Mr. G. R. GEARY (South Toronto) moved the second reading of and concurrence in the amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 29, to amend and consolidate the several acts relating to the Board of Trade of the City of Toronto.
Motion agreed to; amendment read the second time and concurred in.
The house resumed from Friday, April 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Power for the second reading of Bill No. 67, with respect to hospital sweepstakes.

Mr. Speaker, when the hour for private bills expired on Friday last I had just completed a reference to the prevalence of speculation and gambling in the stock markets and had started to refer to the gambling carried on in our grain exchanges. I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that the speculation and gambling carried on in this and other countries during recent years have played a very large part in bringing about the depression now existing. I have given extracts from the evidence adduced in England before a commission dealing with a proposed sweepstake measure. I gave extracts from the evidence given by the representatives of the Church of Scotland and the Christian Social Council of England. I have had submitted to me the opinion of the United Church of Canada, and I should like to refer to a letter written by the Reverend D. N. McLachlan, the secretary of the Board of Evangelism and Social Service of the United Church of Canada. Mr. McLachlan points out, first, that the sweepstakes proposal is economically unsound and, second, that the principle is morally unsound. He continues :
The better elements of Canadian citizens view with regret and misgiving this backward step proposed by the Senate and are depending on the members of parliament to defend the honour of Canada by defeating the bill to legalize sweepstakes in this dominion.
I should like to quote from a resolution passed by the Kindersley presbytery of the United Church of Canada, as follows:
In the move to change the Criminal Code to permit the conducting of sweepstakes for the support of hospitals; this presbytery believing that the result would be a widespread development of the gambling spirit, which would more than offset any advantages which might be derived therefrom, strongly protests against any such action.

Hospital Siveepstakes
That resolution is signed by H. Craner, secretary, Coleville, Saskatchewan.
Every afternoon before the commencement of business in this house Your Honour reads a form of prayer, one day in English and the next in French. In the third clause of that prayer you, sir, invoke the Deity that He "be pleased to direct and prosper all their consultations," referring to the House of Commons:
That all things may be so ordered and settled by their endeavours, upon the best and surest foundations, that peace and happiness, truth and justice, religion and piety, may be established among us for all generations.
That is a very worthy sentiment, but the proposal of this sweepstakes bill is diametrically opposed to the sentiment expressed in that feeling prayer of yours as uttered every day in this chamber.
The sponsor of this bill asked: Why not let people gamble?-they have the gambling spirit anyway. He tried to impress upon us-[DOT] and he did not make a very good job of it, I will admit-that everybody is addicted to the gambling fever, so why not give him a chance to gamble? I challenge that statement; I claim it is not correct. Every person is not addicted to gambling and gambling is not a natural instinct. It would be just as sensible to say in this chamber that opium smoking on the part of a Chinaman was a natural habit and we might as well let him smoke his opium. So far as giving peace and exhilarating joy and transporting the individual into the realms of ecstasy and feelings of inward satisfaction are concerned, I am told nothing surpasses the smoking of the opium pipe. If such be the case, why deprive the poor Chinaman of that wonderful peace and satisfaction of mind which he has as a result of sm oking opium ?
The sponsor of this bill says that because some people get a little satisfaction out of gambling, we should throw the door wide open and let them gamble; they are raised to such heights of joy; they are given such wonderful feelings of ecstasy, it would be too bad to deprive them of that. But we do not assume that attitude towards the Chinaman who takes his long pipe and endeavours to smoke opium. We have legislation that applies to such a person and we take good care that he is restricted in his operations with the opium pipe. So, believing as I do that this bill is a retrograde step in our legislative enactments, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), the following amendment:
That the word "now" be left out and the words "this day six months" added at the end of the question.

Mr. Speaker, may I offer a few observations in regard to this bill? In the first place the proposal embodied in it is purely and simply gambling. It undertakes to legalize what, under our criminal code, is recognized as illegal. In other words, if I understand the matter correctly, the object of the bill is to give respectability to what is generally understood as an illegal undertaking in Canada, something that is made illegal under our criminal code. Gambling of all kinds is objectionable and this form of it is not any exception to the rule. It is well understood that during the last several years, particularly in 1928 and 1929, gambling was the great evil of this country and the source of most of the troubles from which we are now suffering. Particularly is this so in regard to many of our young people, and yet we are undertaking under this bill to make respectable that which we know introduced many of the troubles from which we are now suffering.
Another feature of the bill is that it throws around the ev il of gambling a certain mantle of virtue by introducing some benefit or presumed benefit on behalf of the hospitals. I am ready to admit that it is possible hospitals may be immediately benefited, financially speaking, but I am also firmly convinced that ultimately they will suffer financially as well as otherwise. At present in all parts of our country hospitals are benefited by the donations of the people and also very largely by contributions from estates. Even to-day where the formerly established practices in the administration of hospitals have been interfered with in one way or another by the state, there has been a decided tendency on the part of many people of means not to make in their wills provision for extending donations to hospitals. If gambling, presumably to assist hospitals, becomes law, I am certain this will in the long run be detrimental, financially speaking, to the hospitals. Certainly it will drive away from them a great deal of sympathetic support which they now receive and which they require.
